items.title: Judge Gives Final Approval of $1.5 Billion Anthropic Settlement
items.excerpt: Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted final approval to the landmark $1.5 billion settlement over Anthropic's use of pirated books to train its models. Roughly 500,000 titles were downloaded illegally; 92% of eligible authors and publishers opted in, at about $3,000 per infringed work.

items.title: Court Grants Final Approval to Landmark $1.5 Billion Anthropic Settlement
items.excerpt: A federal judge finalized the $1.5 billion Anthropic copyright settlement, with authors eligible for up to $3,000 per work and larger publishers standing to receive tens of millions. Anthropic must destroy the pirated dataset as a condition of the deal.

items.title: Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement approved
items.excerpt: The US District Court for the Northern District of California granted final approval of the class settlement in Bartz v. Anthropic, resolving the largest copyright class action in US history over books used as AI training data.

items.title: Anthropic settlement approved
items.excerpt: Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin gave final approval to the US$1.5 billion settlement in the class action brought against Anthropic in 2024 for copyright infringement in building its large language models.

items.title: Bloomsbury lands £14m in Anthropic AI settlement
items.excerpt: Bloomsbury has secured roughly $18.7m (£14m) from the Anthropic copyright settlement, one of the first concrete figures showing what an individual trade publisher recovers when its catalogue is used as AI training data.

items.title: Publishers file massive lawsuit against Google Gemini training
items.excerpt: Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning and Elsevier filed a copyright infringement suit accusing Google of unlawfully using copyrighted books to train Gemini. The suit seeks statutory damages and destruction of all unauthorized copies used in training.

items.title: US publishers file lawsuit against Google for 'training Gemini on copyrighted books'
items.excerpt: Publishers and authors launched legal action against Google, alleging widespread copyright violation in using authors' works to develop the Gemini models.

items.title: Publishers Launch New Lawsuit Against Google for Using Digital Books to Train AI
items.excerpt: A group of publishers and author Scott Turow allege Google used books from Google Scholar, Google Books and Google Play well beyond their 'express and agreed upon uses' to train AI — a case built on contract terms rather than scraping alone.

items.title: Substack adds AI detection tools, but creators can disable them
items.excerpt: Substack rolled out AI-detection labelling powered by Pangram so readers can see whether a post was AI-assisted — but writers can switch the badge off entirely, making disclosure effectively opt-in.

items.title: Some Listeners Prefer AI Narration for Multi-Voice Audiobooks
items.excerpt: A survey by AI audiobook company Spoken found 61% of listeners mistook AI narration for human voices in character-driven fiction, with similar numbers favouring AI for multi-character scenes — even as broader willingness to try AI narration fell from 70% to 61%.

items.title: Wiley Joins 'Genesis Mission Consortium' in Support of U.S. AI Goals
items.excerpt: Wiley is the only scientific publisher inside the US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission Consortium, joining Nvidia, AWS, Microsoft, IBM and AMD to supply peer-reviewed content for 'AI-accelerated innovation and discovery'.

items.title: Guest Post — Research Needs a Shared Standard for AI Disclosure
items.excerpt: The World Conference on Research Integrity launched a Focus Track to build unified guidelines for disclosing AI use in scholarly work, after a 2026 survey found about a third of researchers have never disclosed their AI usage when publishing.

items.title: Open Science 2.0: Building Understanding in an AI-Mediated World
items.excerpt: With AI chat interfaces increasingly mediating how readers meet research, the authors argue Open Science 2.0 must design for trust, interpretation and communication — not just open access to the PDF.

items.title: AI dominates global publishing conversation at IPA Congress
items.excerpt: Generative AI was the biggest topic across panels at the International Publishers Congress in Kuala Lumpur, from licensing books as training data to how houses restructure editorial and production work around AI.

items.title: Industry bodies welcome prime minister's comments on AI and copyright
items.excerpt: The Australian Publishers Association and Australian Society of Authors backed PM Anthony Albanese's statement that no company should use Australian books, art or news to train AI without the artist's permission.

items.title: 2026 Annual Conference Wrap-Up
items.excerpt: ALA's sesquicentennial conference in Chicago drew 14,800 attendees, with AI running through the programme: panelists pushed practical library AI services and warned that 'disengagement from AI guarantees your vulnerability' when teaching media literacy.
